summary:
Johor is one of Malaysia's thirteen states and stands under the national framework: federal law criminalises same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity across the country, and the state layer adds Sharia offences that reach Muslims alone. Sections 377A to 377D of the federal Penal Code, in force in Johor, punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and "outrages on decency" with up to twenty years' imprisonment plus whipping. The provisions cover oral and anal sex, apply to men and women alike, reach acts that are consensual and private, and are not confined to Malaysian citizens.

Johor's Sharia enactment sits alongside that federal layer, prohibiting cross-dressing and "males posing as females" together with liwat and musahaqah, with penalties reaching three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These offences apply only to Muslims; a non-Muslim visitor falls under the federal Penal Code alone. The enactments contain no legal definition of transgender dress, so the boundary between compliant and offending presentation is set by officers on the ground.

In November 2023 the Johor state government announced plans to establish conversion-therapy centres to "rehabilitate" LGBT people. The announcement sits within a nationwide crackdown that has run since the 2018 general election: at least 1,733 people had attended state "rehabilitation programmes" as of June 2021. A visitor who comes to the attention of Johor's religious authorities as gender-nonconforming can therefore expect to be routed into a religious intervention rather than a purely legal process.

Enforcement is discretionary rather than systematic. Consenting adults in private are rarely prosecuted under the federal sections, but that discretion is not a legal protection and has been withdrawn at moments of political pressure, most visibly in the mass venue raids documented elsewhere in Malaysia since 2018. There is no explicit visa or entry rule keyed to gender identity; the nearest documented statement of entry policy is a 2001 declaration by then-Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad that Malaysia would deport any visiting foreign cabinet minister or diplomat who is gay.

Malaysian law provides no protection against discrimination or hate crimes on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation, and same-sex marriage and partner recognition are unavailable nationwide. Legal challenges have failed to remove the framework: the Federal Court struck down a Selangor cross-dressing provision in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds only, and nothing under the federal Penal Code has been decriminalised.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters reported on 10 August 2022 that state-conducted investigations into LGBT people covered seven Malaysian states, namely Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah, confirming that the post-2018 crackdown is national in reach rather than confined to any one administration. Johor's own conversion-therapy announcement of November 2023 places the state within that wider pattern.

The same reporting notes that Sharia codes in the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya criminalise same-sex activity and gender nonconformity, so the parallel federal-territory regime is a further data point alongside the state enactments. Federal enforcement patterns documented elsewhere, including raids on social venues and mass arrests under section 377B, indicate how quickly prosecutorial discretion in Johor can harden.

The broader regional comparison is that every one of Malaysia's thirteen states plus the federal territories maintains Sharia offences against cross-dressing, with documented cases of repeated arrests of individual trans women, a mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding in June 2014, and strip-searches by religious officials in detention. Violence against trans women has been lethal and largely unpunished, including a killing in Klang in June 2019 that was the third such killing in under two months.
localsOnly:
The Johor Sharia enactment binds Muslim residents of the state, who may be investigated and prosecuted by the state Islamic religious department for cross-dressing, liwat or musahaqah, with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, an RM5,000 fine and six strokes of caning. Sharia courts may also commit women convicted of musahaqah to an approved home for up to six months and may order other offenders into counselling or rehabilitation in a religious institution for up to six months.

Identity documents are controlled by the state. The Registration Department routinely rejects gender-marker changes, applying a 1982 National Fatwa Committee edict that sex is determined at birth and unaffected by reassignment surgery. The edict was never gazetted and is not legally binding, but it is applied in practice, including to invalidate marriages involving transgender people. A 2016 Kuala Lumpur High Court judgment ordering the National Registration Department to update a trans man's identity card, reasoning that Article 5(1) of the Federal Constitution guarantees a right to live with dignity in one's gender, was overturned on appeal in 2017.

The only documented successful marker change has a Johor connection: in 1975 the Registration Department recognised Sari Kartina binti Abdul Karim as female and the Johor Deputy Mufti permitted her to marry under Sharia law. Whether that precedent remains operative is not established by these sources.

Residents also face the announced conversion-therapy infrastructure: at least 1,733 people had attended state "rehabilitation programmes" as of June 2021, under a crackdown running since the 2018 election, and Johor signalled in November 2023 that it intended to open dedicated centres. No anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection exists on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the conversion-therapy centres announced by the Johor government in November 2023 have been built, staffed or used is unresolved on these sources; only the announcement and the national figure of 1,733 rehabilitation-programme attendees as of June 2021 are sourced.

No Johor-specific arrest, prosecution or sentencing statistics for sections 377A to 377D or for the state Sharia offences are available in this inventory, so the frequency of enforcement in Johor itself is not sourced. The pattern of venue raids and mass arrests cited here is documented for other Malaysian locations.

An explicit entry or visa rule keyed to transgender visitors is not sourced for Malaysia. The 2001 statement by Mahathir Mohamad concerns gay foreign officials rather than trans travellers generally, and no Johor-level entry control has been identified.

Whether the 1975 Registration Department and Johor Deputy Mufti decision on Sari Kartina binti Abdul Karim has any continuing legal effect is unresolved, and no sourced record shows it being followed in the decades since.
